concepts.title: Spring's Arrival in Light and Song
concepts.definition: Larkin's short lyric paints an English spring evening: longer light, chill and yellow, bathing the serene foreheads of houses, a thrush singing in laurel. The poem's music enacts the season's freshness -- innocence arriving with the birdsong.
concepts.key_idea: Spring enters as light and thrush-song -- the season's freshness painted in a few chilled, golden strokes.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww113.txt opening stanzas (longer evenings, light chill and yellow, foreheads of houses, thrush singing laurel surrounded)

solution_steps.explain: Longer, chill, yellow light marks the season's turn -- spring's first signature is lengthening evenings.
Light bathes the 'foreheads' of houses -- personification lending the street a serene, childlike calm.
The thrush, laurel-surrounded, begins its song -- spring's voice entering the poem.

concepts.title: Childhood's Forgotten Wounds and the Coming of Happiness
concepts.definition: Against the spring scene the speaker recalls childhood, whose tears he has forgotten, and confesses a pointless, dull ache that becomes unspent joy. Now the birdsong bridles with fresh joy -- happiness arrives from outside, an alien thing the adult can only watch, like a child at a window.
concepts.key_idea: Happiness comes as a stranger to the adult -- spring's joy witnessed through glass, remembered childhood tears left behind.

solution_steps.explain: The speaker turns back to childhood -- laughter and forgotten tears -- an ache that has no clear cause.
Into this dullness the season's joy arrives, brimming in the birdsong, fresh and unspent.
Like a child watching through a window, the adult observes happiness from outside -- moved, but apart.

concepts.title: Craft of the Lyric: Small Stanzas and the Thrush's Phrase
concepts.definition: Larkin builds the poem in three compact stanzas whose clipped phrases and simple rhymes mirror the quick arrival of spring; the thrush's repeated phrase becomes the poem's own music, so that the lyric's shape performs the season it describes.
concepts.key_idea: Short stanzas and a recurring bird-phrase -- the lyric's form mimics spring's quick, singing arrival.

solution_steps.explain: Three small stanzas move the poem from garden light to memory to the window's hope.
The thrush's beginning-to-start-again phrase recurs, binding the stanzas like a musical motif.
Clipped lines and plain rhymes keep the lyric brisk -- form matching the freshness it celebrates.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the image of happiness as 'an alien thing' that the speaker watches through a window.

solution_template.explain: The joy belongs to the season and to childhood, not to the adult speaker's inner weather.
The window separates watcher from scene -- participation is refused by memory and habit.
Larkin renders happiness as real but unreachable -- seen plainly, felt at a distance.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Comment on the phrase 'Light, chill and yellow' as a description of spring.

solution_template.explain: Chill and yellow hold winter's memory and summer's promise at once -- spring is the hinge season.
The short, clipped phrases mime the lightness of the evenings.
Three adjectives carry the whole scene -- compression that is itself the season's freshness.
